arrays.name: Arrays
arrays.theoryRecap: An array is a collection of elements stored at contiguous memory locations. It allows random access using indices (0-based in most languages). Arrays have fixed size in languages like Java (use ArrayList for dynamic sizing). Key operations: Access O(1), Search O(n), Insert/Delete O(n) due to shifting.

patterns.name: Two Pointers
patterns.description: Use two pointers moving towards each other or in the same direction to solve problems in O(n) time.
patterns.whenToUse: Sorted arrays, finding pairs, palindrome checks, removing duplicates
patterns.example: Two Sum II (sorted), Container With Most Water, Remove Duplicates

patterns.name: Sliding Window
patterns.description: Maintain a window of elements and slide it across the array to find subarrays meeting certain conditions.
patterns.whenToUse: Finding subarrays with specific sum, longest/shortest subarray with condition
patterns.example: Maximum Subarray, Minimum Window Substring, Longest Substring Without Repeating

patterns.name: Prefix Sum
patterns.description: Precompute cumulative sums to answer range sum queries in O(1).
patterns.whenToUse: Range sum queries, subarray sum equals K
patterns.example: Range Sum Query, Subarray Sum Equals K, Product of Array Except Self

patterns.name: Kadane's Algorithm
patterns.description: Track maximum sum ending at each position to find maximum subarray sum in O(n).
patterns.whenToUse: Maximum subarray problems
patterns.example: Maximum Subarray, Maximum Product Subarray

codeTemplates.name: Two Pointers Template
Sliding Window Template
Prefix Sum Template

analogies.analogy: A row of lockers in a school - each locker has a number (index) and you can directly go to any locker without checking others.
Two people searching for each other in a hallway - one starts from left, one from right, they walk towards each other until they meet.
Looking through a magnifying glass that you slide across a newspaper - you can only see a portion at a time, but you move it to see everything.

commonMistakes.description: Using <= instead of < in loops, or starting from 1 instead of 0
commonMistakes.fix: Always double-check loop bounds. arr.length gives count, last index is arr.length - 1

commonMistakes.description: Accessing arr[0] when array might be empty causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
commonMistakes.fix: Always check if (arr == null || arr.length == 0) at the start

commonMistakes.description: Removing elements while looping forward causes skipped elements
commonMistakes.fix: Iterate backwards when removing, or use iterator.remove()

commonMistakes.description: Using (left + right) / 2 can overflow for large values
commonMistakes.fix: Use left + (right - left) / 2 instead

flashcards.front: Time complexity to access element at index i?
flashcards.back: O(1) - Direct access using memory address calculation

flashcards.front: Why is insertion O(n) in arrays?
flashcards.back: All elements after insertion point must be shifted right

flashcards.front: What is the Two Pointer technique?
flashcards.back: Using two indices that move towards each other or in same direction to solve problems efficiently

flashcards.front: When to use Sliding Window?
flashcards.back: When finding subarrays/substrings with specific properties (sum, length, contents)

flashcards.front: What does prefix[j] - prefix[i] give?
flashcards.back: Sum of elements from index i to j-1 in the original array

flashcards.front: How do you find the middle element of an array?
flashcards.back: Use index: startIndex + (endIndex - startIndex) / 2 to avoid overflow

flashcards.front: Space complexity of creating a 2D array of size N x M?
flashcards.back: O(N * M) - proportional to the total number of elements

flashcards.front: When is an array NOT appropriate to use?
flashcards.back: When you need frequent insertions/deletions or don't know the size in advance

strings.name: Strings
strings.theoryRecap: Strings are sequences of characters. In Java, strings are immutable - any modification creates a new string. Use StringBuilder for efficient concatenation. Common operations involve character frequency counting, substring matching, and palindrome checking.

patterns.name: Character Frequency
patterns.description: Count occurrences of each character using array[26] for lowercase or HashMap for any characters.
patterns.whenToUse: Anagrams, character counting, finding duplicates
patterns.example: Valid Anagram, First Unique Character, Group Anagrams

patterns.name: Two Pointers for Strings
patterns.description: Use left and right pointers for palindrome checks or string reversal.
patterns.whenToUse: Palindrome verification, string reversal, comparing characters from both ends
patterns.example: Valid Palindrome, Reverse String

patterns.name: Sliding Window for Substrings
patterns.description: Track characters in current window to find substrings with specific properties.
patterns.whenToUse: Longest substring problems, minimum window problems
patterns.example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Minimum Window Substring

codeTemplates.name: Character Frequency Array
Palindrome Check
StringBuilder for Concatenation

analogies.analogy: Like a printed book - you can't change a word on a page, you have to print a new book with the change.
Like a whiteboard - you can erase and write new things without creating a new board.
Like rearranging letter tiles in Scrabble - same letters, different arrangement.

commonMistakes.description: == compares references, not content
commonMistakes.fix: Always use str1.equals(str2) for content comparison

commonMistakes.description: Creates new String object each iteration - O(n²) total
commonMistakes.fix: Use StringBuilder.append() in loops

commonMistakes.description: Calling methods on null string causes NullPointerException
commonMistakes.fix: Check if (str != null && !str.isEmpty()) first

flashcards.front: Why are Java strings immutable?
flashcards.back: Security, thread-safety, and string pool optimization

flashcards.front: Difference between String and StringBuilder?
flashcards.back: String is immutable (new object per change), StringBuilder is mutable (same object)

flashcards.front: How to check if two strings are anagrams?
flashcards.back: Compare sorted characters or character frequency arrays

flashcards.front: Time complexity of String concatenation?
flashcards.back: O(n) per operation - it creates a new string each time

flashcards.front: How does Java store Strings efficiently?
flashcards.back: Using the String Constant Pool (interning) to reuse identical string literals

flashcards.front: What is the time complexity of substring() in Java?
flashcards.back: O(n) in newer Java versions (copies characters), was O(1) in older versions (shared array)

flashcards.front: How to convert a String to an integer?
flashcards.back: Integer.parseInt(str) or Integer.valueOf(str)

hashmaps.name: HashMap & HashSet
hashmaps.theoryRecap: HashMap stores key-value pairs with O(1) average time for get/put operations. It uses hashing to compute the index where values are stored. HashSet is similar but only stores unique keys (no values). Collisions are handled via chaining or open addressing.

patterns.name: Frequency Counting
patterns.description: Count occurrences of elements using map.getOrDefault()
patterns.whenToUse: Finding duplicates, top K frequent, word count
patterns.example: Top K Frequent Elements, First Unique Character

patterns.name: Two Sum Pattern
patterns.description: Store complement values to find pairs in O(n)
patterns.whenToUse: Finding pairs that sum to target, finding matching elements
patterns.example: Two Sum, 4Sum, Subarray Sum Equals K

patterns.name: Grouping/Bucketing
patterns.description: Group elements by a computed key
patterns.whenToUse: Grouping anagrams, grouping by property
patterns.example: Group Anagrams, Repeated DNA Sequences

codeTemplates.name: Frequency Counter
Two Sum Pattern
HashSet for Duplicates

analogies.analogy: Like a library catalog - you have the book title (key) and it instantly tells you the shelf location (value).
Like assigning students to lockers based on their roll number - each number maps to a specific locker.
Two students assigned the same locker - they need to share or find another way (chaining).

commonMistakes.description: If key object changes, hash changes, can't find the value
commonMistakes.fix: Use immutable keys (String, Integer) or don't modify key objects

commonMistakes.description: map.get() returns null for missing keys
commonMistakes.fix: Use getOrDefault() or containsKey() check

commonMistakes.description: Custom objects won't work correctly in HashMap
commonMistakes.fix: Always override both hashCode() and equals() together

flashcards.front: Average time complexity of HashMap get()?
flashcards.back: O(1) - direct access via hash computation

flashcards.front: What happens during a hash collision?
flashcards.back: Multiple entries stored at same index using chaining (linked list) or probing

flashcards.front: HashMap vs TreeMap?
flashcards.back: HashMap: O(1) unordered. TreeMap: O(log n) sorted by keys

flashcards.front: When does HashMap become O(n)?
flashcards.back: When all keys hash to same bucket (worst case collision)

flashcards.front: What is the default load factor of a HashMap?
flashcards.back: 0.75 - it resizes when 75% full to balance space and time

flashcards.front: Can you use null as a key in HashMap?
flashcards.back: Yes, HashMap allows one null key (stored at index 0), but Hashtable does not

flashcards.front: How to iterate over a HashMap?
flashcards.back: Use map.entrySet(), map.keySet(), or map.values() in a loop

linkedlist.name: Linked List
linkedlist.theoryRecap: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are connected via pointers. Each node contains data and a reference to the next node. Unlike arrays, linked lists allow efficient O(1) insertions/deletions at known positions but have O(n) access time.

patterns.name: Two Pointers (Fast & Slow)
patterns.description: Use two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles or find middle.
patterns.whenToUse: Cycle detection, finding middle, finding nth from end
patterns.example: Linked List Cycle, Middle of Linked List, Remove Nth Node From End

patterns.name: Dummy Head
patterns.description: Create a dummy node before head to simplify edge cases.
patterns.whenToUse: When head might change, merging lists, removing nodes
patterns.example: Merge Two Sorted Lists, Remove Duplicates, Partition List

patterns.name: Reversal
patterns.description: Reverse links by changing next pointers iteratively or recursively.
patterns.whenToUse: Reverse entire list or portions of it
patterns.example: Reverse Linked List, Reverse Nodes in k-Group

codeTemplates.name: Fast & Slow Pointer (Cycle Detection)
Reverse Linked List
Dummy Head Pattern

analogies.analogy: Like a treasure hunt - each clue (node) tells you where the next clue is located.
Like a train - each car knows both the car in front and behind it.
Like a race track - if there's a loop, the faster runner will eventually catch up to the slower one.

timeComplexity.insertAtEnd: O(n) or O(1) with tail pointer
timeComplexity.delete: O(1) if node given, O(n) to find

commonMistakes.description: Moving head pointer without saving it first
commonMistakes.fix: Use a separate curr pointer to traverse, keep head intact

commonMistakes.description: Accessing node.next.next without checking node.next
commonMistakes.fix: Always check if (node != null && node.next != null)

commonMistakes.description: Code breaks when list has only 1 element
commonMistakes.fix: Test edge cases: empty list, single node, two nodes

flashcards.front: Time to access nth element in linked list?
flashcards.back: O(n) - must traverse from head

flashcards.front: What's the fast & slow pointer technique?
flashcards.back: Two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles or find middle

flashcards.front: How to reverse a linked list in-place?
flashcards.back: Use three pointers: prev, curr, next. Change curr.next to prev, move all forward

flashcards.front: Array vs LinkedList for insertions?
flashcards.back: LinkedList O(1) at known position, Array O(n) due to shifting

flashcards.front: What is a 'Runner' pointer?
flashcards.back: A second pointer (often faster) used to compare or look ahead (e.g., detecting cycles)

flashcards.front: Space complexity of a recursive linked list reversal?
flashcards.back: O(n) due to the function call stack

flashcards.front: Difference between Singly and Doubly Linked List?
flashcards.back: Singly has next pointer; Doubly has next and prev pointers (more memory, easier backward traversal)

stacks.name: Stack
stacks.theoryRecap: A stack is a LIFO (Last In, First Out) data structure. Think of a stack of plates - you add and remove from the top only. Main operations: push (add to top), pop (remove from top), peek (view top). Stacks are used for function calls, undo operations, and expression evaluation.

patterns.name: Monotonic Stack
patterns.description: Maintain a stack where elements are in increasing or decreasing order.
patterns.whenToUse: Next greater/smaller element, stock span, histogram problems
patterns.example: Next Greater Element, Daily Temperatures, Largest Rectangle in Histogram

patterns.name: Matching Pairs
patterns.description: Use stack to match opening and closing elements.
patterns.whenToUse: Valid parentheses, HTML tag matching, expression evaluation
patterns.example: Valid Parentheses, Decode String, Basic Calculator

patterns.name: Expression Evaluation
patterns.description: Use stack(s) to evaluate infix, prefix, or postfix expressions.
patterns.whenToUse: Calculator problems, parsing expressions
patterns.example: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, Basic Calculator II

codeTemplates.name: Valid Parentheses
Monotonic Stack (Next Greater)

analogies.analogy: Stack of plates in a cafeteria - you can only take from or add to the top.
Like nested Russian dolls - you must close the inner one before closing the outer one.
Like Ctrl+Z in a text editor - it undoes the most recent action first.

commonMistakes.description: EmptyStackException if stack.pop() on empty stack
commonMistakes.fix: Always check !stack.isEmpty() before pop()

commonMistakes.description: Java Stack class is synchronized and slower
commonMistakes.fix: Use Deque<> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); instead

flashcards.front: What does LIFO mean?
flashcards.back: Last In, First Out - most recently added element is removed first

flashcards.front: Time complexity of push and pop?
flashcards.back: Both O(1) - operations only happen at top

flashcards.front: What is a monotonic stack?
flashcards.back: A stack maintaining elements in sorted order (all increasing or all decreasing)

flashcards.front: Real-world use of stacks?
flashcards.back: Browser back button, undo/redo, function call stack

flashcards.front: What data structure implements a recursive algorithm iteratively?
flashcards.back: A Stack

flashcards.front: How to implement a Queue using Stacks?
flashcards.back: Use two stacks: one for push(in), one for pop(out). Move elements when out-stack is empty.

flashcards.front: Time complexity to find the minimum element in a standard stack?
flashcards.back: O(n) - you must traverse the whole stack. O(1) if using a MinStack design.

queues.name: Queue
queues.theoryRecap: A queue is a FIFO (First In, First Out) data structure. Think of a line at a store - first person in line is first to be served. Main operations: enqueue (add to back), dequeue (remove from front). Used in BFS, task scheduling, and buffering.

patterns.name: BFS with Queue
patterns.description: Use queue to explore nodes level by level.
patterns.whenToUse: Shortest path in unweighted graph, level order traversal
patterns.example: Binary Tree Level Order, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix, Rotting Oranges

patterns.name: Sliding Window Maximum
patterns.description: Use deque to maintain candidates for maximum in current window.
patterns.whenToUse: Finding max/min in sliding window efficiently
patterns.example: Sliding Window Maximum, Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K

codeTemplates.name: BFS Template
Level Order Traversal

analogies.analogy: Line at a movie theater - first person in line gets served first.
Like ripples in water - explore all nearby points before going further.
Hospital ER - patients treated by urgency, not arrival time.

commonMistakes.description: add() throws exception on failure, offer() returns false
commonMistakes.fix: Use offer() for safer code, especially with bounded queues

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to mark visited in BFS
commonMistakes.description: Causes infinite loops in graphs with cycles
commonMistakes.fix: Always mark node as visited when adding to queue, not when processing

flashcards.front: What does FIFO mean?
flashcards.back: First In, First Out - first element added is first removed

flashcards.front: Difference between offer() and add()?
flashcards.back: offer() returns false on failure, add() throws exception

flashcards.front: When to use Queue vs Stack?
flashcards.back: Queue for BFS/level order, Stack for DFS/backtracking

flashcards.front: What is a Priority Queue?
flashcards.back: Queue where elements are ordered by priority, not insertion order

flashcards.front: Time complexity of enqueue and dequeue?
flashcards.back: O(1) - constant time operations

flashcards.front: What is a Deque?
flashcards.back: Double-ended queue: can add/remove from both front and rear

flashcards.front: How to implement a Stack using Queues?
flashcards.back: Using 1 queue (push -> rotate size-1 times) or 2 queues

trees.name: Binary Trees
trees.theoryRecap: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children (left and right). Key concepts: root (top node), leaf (no children), height (longest path to leaf), depth (distance from root). Traversals: Inorder (L-Root-R), Preorder (Root-L-R), Postorder (L-R-Root).

patterns.name: DFS Traversal
patterns.description: Explore as deep as possible before backtracking. Use recursion or explicit stack.
patterns.whenToUse: Path problems, tree structure problems, serialization
patterns.example: Maximum Depth, Path Sum, Same Tree

patterns.name: BFS Level Order
patterns.description: Explore all nodes at current level before moving to next level using queue.
patterns.whenToUse: Level-wise processing, finding minimum depth, zigzag traversal
patterns.example: Level Order Traversal, Minimum Depth, Right Side View

patterns.name: Recursive Structure
patterns.description: Solve problem for subtrees and combine results.
patterns.whenToUse: Most tree problems - think of base case and how to combine left/right results
patterns.example: Maximum Depth, Balanced Tree, Diameter

codeTemplates.name: Recursive DFS Template
Inorder Traversal
Level Order BFS

analogies.analogy: Family tree - each person (node) can have at most two children.
Delegating work - 'Ask my left and right children for their answers, then combine.'
Organized bookshelf - smaller books on left, larger on right, making search fast.

timeComplexity.search: O(n) general, O(log n) BST balanced
timeComplexity.insert: O(n) general, O(log n) BST balanced

cheatSheet.spaceComplexity: O(h) for recursion stack, h = height
bestFor: Binary Search Tree for sorted data

commonMistakes.description: NullPointerException when accessing node.left or node.val on null
commonMistakes.fix: Always check if (node == null) return ... at start of recursive function

commonMistakes.description: Mixing up inorder (L-N-R), preorder (N-L-R), postorder (L-R-N)
commonMistakes.fix: Remember: 'in' = node in middle, 'pre' = node first, 'post' = node last

commonMistakes.mistake: Not using return value in recursion
commonMistakes.description: Recursive call made but result ignored
commonMistakes.fix: return solve(node.left) - don't forget to capture/use the returned value

flashcards.front: What is inorder traversal order?
flashcards.back: Left → Node → Right. For BST, this gives sorted order.

flashcards.front: Height vs Depth of a node?
flashcards.back: Height: distance to farthest leaf. Depth: distance from root.

flashcards.front: Time complexity to find element in BST?
flashcards.back: O(log n) average (balanced), O(n) worst (skewed)

flashcards.front: When to use BFS vs DFS on trees?
flashcards.back: BFS for level-wise problems, DFS for path/depth problems

dp.name: Dynamic Programming
dp.theoryRecap: Dynamic Programming solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each once, and storing the results. Two approaches: Top-down (recursion + memoization) and Bottom-up (iterative with table). Key: identify the state, recurrence relation, and base cases.

patterns.name: 1D DP
patterns.description: State depends on previous elements in a single dimension.
patterns.whenToUse: Climbing stairs, house robber, fibonacci-like problems
patterns.example: Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Decode Ways

patterns.name: 2D DP
patterns.description: State depends on two dimensions (often two strings or a grid).
patterns.whenToUse: String matching, grid paths, subsequence problems
patterns.example: Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Unique Paths

patterns.name: Knapsack Pattern
patterns.description: Select items with constraints (weight/capacity) to maximize value.
patterns.whenToUse: Subset sum, coin change, partition problems
patterns.example: 0/1 Knapsack, Coin Change, Partition Equal Subset Sum

patterns.name: Interval DP
patterns.description: Combine results from subproblems within intervals.
patterns.whenToUse: Matrix chain multiplication, burst balloons, palindrome partitioning
patterns.example: Burst Balloons, Palindrome Partitioning II

codeTemplates.name: 1D DP Template
2D DP Template (LCS)
Memoization Template

analogies.analogy: Like writing down answers to math problems - if asked again, just look it up instead of recalculating.
Like fib(5) needing fib(3) and fib(4), but fib(4) also needs fib(3) - same subproblem appears multiple times.
If the best route from A to C goes through B, it must use the best route from A to B.

timeComplexity.depends: On number of states × time per state

commonMistakes.description: Unclear what dp[i] represents leads to wrong recurrence
commonMistakes.fix: Write down in words: 'dp[i] = maximum profit using first i items'

commonMistakes.description: Forgetting dp[0] initialization or edge cases
commonMistakes.fix: Think: what's the answer for smallest valid input?

commonMistakes.description: Computing dp[i] before its dependencies are ready
commonMistakes.fix: Ensure all dp values needed for current cell are already computed

commonMistakes.description: Confusing 0-indexed string with 1-indexed dp table
commonMistakes.fix: Use dp[i][j] for first i and j characters, access s.charAt(i-1)

flashcards.front: What are the two DP approaches?
flashcards.back: Top-down (recursion + memoization) and Bottom-up (iterative tabulation)

flashcards.front: What is optimal substructure?
flashcards.back: Optimal solution to problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems

flashcards.front: What are overlapping subproblems?
flashcards.back: Same subproblems are solved multiple times in naive recursion

flashcards.front: How to identify DP problems?
flashcards.back: Keywords: minimum/maximum, count ways, can you achieve, optimal

graphs.name: Graphs
graphs.theoryRecap: A graph consists of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections). Graphs can be directed/undirected and weighted/unweighted. Represented as adjacency list (Map<Node, List<Node>>) or adjacency matrix. Key algorithms: BFS for shortest path (unweighted), DFS for connectivity, Dijkstra for weighted shortest path.

patterns.name: BFS for Shortest Path
patterns.description: Use queue to explore level by level. First time reaching a node is shortest path.
patterns.whenToUse: Shortest path in unweighted graph, minimum steps/moves
patterns.example: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix, Word Ladder, Rotting Oranges

patterns.name: DFS for Connectivity
patterns.description: Explore as deep as possible. Good for checking if path exists, finding all paths.
patterns.whenToUse: Connected components, cycle detection, path existence
patterns.example: Number of Islands, Clone Graph, Course Schedule

patterns.name: Topological Sort
patterns.description: Order nodes so all dependencies come before dependents.
patterns.whenToUse: Task scheduling, build order, course prerequisites
patterns.example: Course Schedule, Alien Dictionary

patterns.name: Union Find
patterns.description: Efficiently manage disjoint sets and find if elements are connected.
patterns.whenToUse: Connected components, cycle detection in undirected graphs
patterns.example: Number of Connected Components, Redundant Connection

codeTemplates.name: BFS Template
DFS Template
Union Find Template

analogies.analogy: Like a social network - people are nodes, friendships are edges.
Like ripples in a pond - explore all neighbors first before going further.
Like exploring a maze - go as deep as possible, backtrack when stuck.
Like getting dressed - must put on underwear before pants, shirt before jacket.

commonMistakes.description: Infinite loop in graphs with cycles
commonMistakes.fix: Always maintain visited set, mark when adding to queue (BFS) or when entering (DFS)

commonMistakes.description: Missing edges or wrong direction in directed graph
commonMistakes.fix: For undirected: add both (a,b) and (b,a). For directed: only add (a,b)

commonMistakes.description: BFS doesn't find shortest path when edges have different weights
commonMistakes.fix: Use Dijkstra's algorithm for weighted shortest path

flashcards.front: When to use BFS vs DFS?
flashcards.back: BFS: shortest path (unweighted), level order. DFS: path existence, backtracking, cycles

flashcards.front: Time complexity of BFS/DFS?
flashcards.back: O(V + E) where V = vertices, E = edges

flashcards.front: What is topological sort?
flashcards.back: Linear ordering where for every edge (u,v), u comes before v. Only for DAGs.

flashcards.front: Adjacency list vs matrix?
flashcards.back: List: O(V+E) space, O(degree) edge check. Matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge check

binarysearch.name: Binary Search
binarysearch.theoryRecap: Binary Search finds target in sorted array in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search space. Compare target with middle element: if equal, found; if smaller, search left half; if larger, search right half. Can also be used to find boundaries or search in rotated arrays.

patterns.name: Classic Binary Search
patterns.description: Find exact target in sorted array.
patterns.whenToUse: Finding element in sorted array
patterns.example: Binary Search, Search Insert Position

patterns.name: Find Boundary
patterns.description: Find first/last occurrence or boundary where condition changes.
patterns.whenToUse: First bad version, finding peaks, range problems
patterns.example: First Bad Version, Find First and Last Position

patterns.name: Search in Rotated
patterns.description: Modified binary search for rotated sorted arrays.
patterns.whenToUse: Rotated array problems
patterns.example: Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find Minimum in Rotated

patterns.name: Binary Search on Answer
patterns.description: Binary search the answer space, not the input array.
patterns.whenToUse: Minimize maximum, capacity problems
patterns.example: Koko Eating Bananas, Split Array Largest Sum

codeTemplates.name: Classic Binary Search
Find Left Boundary
Binary Search on Answer

analogies.analogy: Finding a word in a dictionary - open to middle, if your word comes before, look in left half.
Guessing a number 1-100 - always guess middle to eliminate half possibilities.

templates.findExact: left <= right, return mid when found
templates.findBoundary: left < right, move boundary based on condition

commonMistakes.description: (left + right) / 2 can overflow for large values
commonMistakes.fix: Use left + (right - left) / 2

commonMistakes.description: Using wrong boundary update leads to endless loop
commonMistakes.fix: Ensure search space shrinks every iteration. If left = mid, use mid + 1

commonMistakes.description: Using wrong condition (< vs <=) or wrong initial bounds
commonMistakes.fix: Think carefully: should right be arr.length or arr.length - 1?

flashcards.front: Time complexity of binary search?
flashcards.back: O(log n) - search space halves each iteration

flashcards.front: Why use left + (right - left) / 2?
flashcards.back: Prevents integer overflow that (left + right) / 2 might cause

flashcards.front: Difference between left <= right and left < right?
flashcards.back: <= for finding exact element, < for finding boundaries

flashcards.front: Can binary search work on unsorted arrays?
flashcards.back: No, array must be sorted or have monotonic property
